answer_text:
Let  
\[
S_N^a=\sum_{n\le N}a_n,\qquad S_N^b=\sum_{n\le N}b_n.
\]
Since \(a_n\sim b_n\), we have
\[
\frac{a_n}{b_n}\to 1.
\]
Write
\[
\frac{a_n}{b_n}=1+c_n,
\]
where \(c_n\to 0\). Then
\[
S_N^a=S_N^b+\sum_{n\le N}c_n b_n.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{S_N^a}{S_N^b}
=1+\frac{\sum_{n\le N}c_n b_n}{S_N^b}.
\]

Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N_0\) such that \(|c_n|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n>N_0\). For \(N>N_0\),
\[
\left|\sum_{n\le N}c_n b_n\right|
\le \sum_{n\le N_0}|c_n|b_n+\varepsilon\sum_{n=N_0+1}^N b_n.
\]
The first term is a constant independent of \(N\). Therefore,
\[
\left|\frac{S_N^a}{S_N^b}-1\right|
\le \frac{C}{S_N^b}+\varepsilon.
\]
Since \(b_n>0\) and \(\sum b_n\) diverges, \(S_N^b\to\infty\), so
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\left|\frac{S_N^a}{S_N^b}-1\right|\le \varepsilon.
\]
Because \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary,
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{n\le N}a_n}{\sum_{n\le N}b_n}=1.
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, the limit is }1.}
\]
